event: UFC Fight Night: Buckley vs. Malott

items.fight_news: Buckley's path improves when he can finish an exchange and regain open space before Malott establishes a grip. Malott's best opportunities may come from attaching a clinch to Buckley's committed punches, then forcing a second defensive action. The useful early read is whether Buckley escapes immediately or remains tied up after stopping the first entry.

Malott should distinguish between a takedown and a sustainable top position. Chasing a submission before controlling Buckley's hips could give the explosive welterweight a route back to his feet. Conversely, short ground strikes that force Buckley to post may create safer back-taking opportunities than a prolonged squeeze on a defended choke.

Rounds four and five remain an important uncertainty for Malott. His recent Burns finish came in round three, so it does not establish a proven 25-minute pace. Repeated failed takedowns and extended submission attempts would increase the cost of his early offense; relaxed clinch work and clean resets would make a later-round fade less convincing.

Buckley does not have to match every minute of positional control if he produces the more damaging offense, but isolated bursts may be insufficient against productive grappling. Watch whether Malott turns holds into strikes or credible submission threats. If he only contains Buckley, the fight may remain much closer than cage position suggests.

The first completed takedown is less informative than the next scramble. Blanchfield can threaten submissions after the position changes, while Jasudavicius has built considerable success from sustained top control. If Jasudavicius has to disengage to protect her neck or arms, her initial wrestling success may not translate into a lasting advantage.

Blanchfield's entries need cover from her striking. Reaching for a clinch from too far away would let Jasudavicius frame, land, and reset before the grappling begins. Closing distance behind combinations could instead force the Canadian to defend the cage approach and the takedown in sequence, reducing her time to establish strong grips.

This co-main event offers only three rounds, so a slow opening carries a greater cost than in Blanchfield's previous five-round assignments. A first round spent testing entries without producing effective offense could leave her needing both remaining rounds. An early successful adjustment matters more here than the ability to sustain a long rally.

bouts.title: Kyle Nelson vs Cristian Perez Gonzalez

items.fight_news: Nelson's accumulated striking rates show more significant strikes absorbed than landed, suggesting that a prolonged exchange-heavy contest is not automatically his safest route. Perez Gonzalez can test that vulnerability by ending combinations with an exit instead of staying for a return trade. Nelson needs his forward movement to produce clean contact or positional gains.

Perez Gonzalez's transition to UFC opposition is a reason to keep confidence modest, even if his opening offense looks sharp. Nelson can test him with clinch pressure followed by strikes on the break. The revealing sequence is whether the newcomer restores his stance and guard after physical exchanges, rather than only how fast he starts.

Barriault's close-range offense creates a specific hazard against Daukaus: leaning forward to continue punching can expose the neck and near arm to a front-headlock attack. Daukaus may not need a clean takedown if he can redirect a clinch into that position. Barriault's head posture and underhook recovery will matter whenever the exchange compresses.

Daukaus can improve his chances by making Barriault defend several connected attacks instead of repeatedly shooting from distance. A failed entry that becomes a clinch or snap-down still asks a question; a failed entry followed by a stationary reset invites Barriault's volume. Watch whether Daukaus can interrupt combinations without spending the whole round backing up.

Barriault's pace can become an advantage if he keeps the exchanges upright and denies long grappling pauses. However, sustained output is expensive when every break requires a hard escape. A drop in combination length after successive clinches would suggest that Daukaus is imposing a larger workload than the visible strike totals capture.

Jourdain's lead-leg attacks can do more than accumulate damage: they can slow Cuamba's exits and make follow-up punches easier to line up. Cuamba needs to answer or reposition before the kicks become uncontested. If Jourdain can kick without absorbing a clean return, his range control becomes more credible as the fight develops.

Cuamba should protect the position before trying to explode out of a scramble. Turning away without controlling Jourdain's hands could allow a transition onto the back; staying square with frames preserves a route to standing. Jourdain's grappling advantage would be easier to trust if he can retain control after Cuamba's first escape attempt.

Cuamba's distance striking has produced more significant strikes absorbed than landed across his UFC sample. A patient countering approach therefore needs visible clean returns to justify low activity. If Jourdain supplies both initiative and effective contact, Cuamba may need to increase output earlier than a finish-focused game plan would prefer.

Nallo has a three-inch listed reach advantage, but that helps only if he makes Landwehr cross dangerous space before exchanging. Straight shots and lateral exits can separate clean offense from a mutual pocket trade. If Landwehr repeatedly reaches chest-to-chest range without taking a meaningful shot, Nallo's length is not controlling the matchup.

Landwehr's pressure can expose Nallo's responses under a sustained workload, yet forward movement also risks walking onto knees or uppercuts. The key distinction is whether Landwehr closes behind offense or simply absorbs contact to get near him. Nallo's early power should carry more predictive weight if he stays balanced enough to defend the next rush.

Nallo's career wins have all been finishes, leaving less evidence for his ability to secure a close UFC decision over three rounds. If the early finish does not materialize, watch whether his output and defensive footwork remain organized. Landwehr can make the later rounds competitive by maintaining effective offense rather than merely surviving.

Diniz has a four-inch listed reach advantage, creating a difficult entry problem for Boser. Boser may need to make him reset with feints and lateral movement before stepping into punching range. If Boser advances straight behind a single shot, Diniz has more opportunity to meet him with a counter before he can exit.

Boser's movement should be judged by whether it creates unanswered scoring exchanges. Circling without landing leaves Diniz free to occupy the center and choose his attacks. Diniz, in turn, needs to cut off exits rather than follow Boser around the perimeter; repeated direction changes would reveal whether that pressure is economical.

Neither fighter's UFC statistical profile shows an established offensive takedown game. A sudden wrestling attempt is therefore a tactical possibility rather than a dependable baseline. If one does complete a takedown, the ability to hold position and land strikes will matter more than assuming the fight has permanently changed into a grappling contest.

Galanti's contract-winning right hook came from close range, making an unprotected clinch entry a meaningful risk for Leblanc. Leblanc can reduce that exposure by connecting his approach to a jab or a level change. Galanti's timing is more threatening if Leblanc repeatedly arrives upright with his hands occupied reaching for grips.

A 35-second showcase provides little evidence about Galanti's response to extended resistance. If Leblanc can survive the first exchanges and force successive clinch breaks, Galanti's recovery between efforts becomes a useful read. Leblanc also needs to preserve safe head position when those breaks become scrambles instead of rushing to stand.

Mahjoub's judo experience suggests a route through body locks and off-balancing, but MMA removes the jacket grips and adds strikes. The first clinch will test that translation. Faglier can make throws harder by keeping his hips back and fighting for inside position; Mahjoub needs to establish control before committing his weight to a turn.

A throw that lands Mahjoub on top would be more informative than an isolated burst of aggression. If he can stabilize and strike, Faglier must solve both the takedown and the ground position. If Faglier immediately stands or reverses, the clinch advantage is less decisive and Mahjoub may pay repeatedly for each attempt.

Cerminara can ask Stiller to cross repeated jabs and kicks before she reaches a usable grip. Stiller's submission threat becomes more relevant once she settles into a controlling position, so the entry and stabilization matter separately. Cerminara should be favored by long stretches of clean distance work, but fewer exchanges alone would not demonstrate effective range control.

Cerminara's lengthy absence creates uncertainty about timing rather than proof of physical decline. Watch her reactions after Stiller's first feints and level changes: balanced counters and immediate exits would reduce that concern. Delayed resets or retreating straight to the fence would give Stiller access to the clinch without requiring a refined distance attack.

Stiller's recent regional bouts were at strawweight, while this assignment is at flyweight. The move may reduce the weight-cut burden but also expose her to a larger, experienced opponent. If she reaches the clinch yet cannot turn or displace Cerminara, her submission skills may remain difficult to bring into play.

Koslow's most important task is securing a position he can retain after Anheliger's first escape. Advancing immediately toward a submission can surrender top control if the veteran creates space. Anheliger, meanwhile, needs to make Koslow restart the entry rather than allowing a failed shot to become an uninterrupted chain of grappling attacks.

Both men return after long UFC absences, which makes old per-minute rates a weak basis for a confident pace forecast. The second round should reveal more: does Koslow keep connecting takedowns after the initial submission opportunity passes, and can Anheliger still create clean combinations after repeated escapes? Those responses matter more than early activity alone.

Croden can test Chandler's defense by pairing straight punches with an angle change before the return exchange. Chandler needs to turn that movement into a physical clinch or force Croden to reset without scoring. If Croden repeatedly lands and leaves untouched, Chandler's forward pressure may be consuming energy without narrowing the striking gap.

Chandler's armbar threat makes extended posting during a scramble hazardous for Croden. Croden should first recover her elbow position and base before trying to stand explosively. Conversely, Chandler risks losing a useful top position if she falls back on an attack without securing the arm; the transition can change both finish risk and round momentum.

Croden has previous late finishes and five-round experience, but that does not guarantee a pace advantage against this opponent. The stronger live indicator is whether she can maintain clean offense after clinch exchanges. Chandler can alter that trajectory by making Croden carry weight and defend grips between the striking exchanges.

You's repeated takedown attempts can test Chovancek's ability to defend beyond the first sprawl. Chovancek needs an underhook and a clear separation, not just a momentary stop, to resume striking on his terms. If You keeps attaching to the hips after being denied, his persistence may matter more than the success rate of individual shots.

Chovancek's debut makes his response to prolonged UFC wrestling difficult to project. Early striking success would be less reassuring if each defensive sequence takes longer to escape. You should improve his prospects if he converts pressure into useful ground offense; ineffective holding would leave Chovancek opportunities to win exchanges after each reset.
